text: Schwartz, Bransford & Sears (2005) introduce the two-dimensional efficiency-vs-innovation framework + Preparation for Future Learning (PFL) as a transfer assessment paradigm distinct from sequestered problem-solving tests.

Kapur (2008) — engaging students in solving complex, ill-structured problems without scaffolding before instruction produces stronger transfer than well-structured-first sequence. Empirical study with 11th-grade Newtonian kinematics.

Barnett & Ceci (2002) — 9-dimensional taxonomy of far transfer (content × context dimensions). Diagnoses why a century of transfer research has failed to resolve "does far transfer exist" — comparisons across studies measured different dimensions without acknowledging it.
Detterman (1993) — the canonical pessimistic argument that little evidence supports transfer of complex school-taught skills. "Transfer as epiphenomenon" reframing.

Synthesizes cognitive-science research on learning and transfer, arguing that transfer depends on degree of mastery, understanding versus memorization, time-on-task, and the representation of the original learning context.
Improvement in one mental function transfers to another only insofar as the two functions share identical elements, undercutting the doctrine of formal discipline and general mental faculties.

Distinguishes low-road transfer (automatic triggering of well-practiced behavior in similar contexts) from high-road transfer (deliberate, mindful abstraction), with forward- and backward-reaching variants.
Experiments show analogical transfer is cued by surface-semantic features but facilitated by inducing a general schema from multiple analogs, separating surface from structural similarity.
Argues the dominant direct-application view of transfer is too narrow and proposes a preparation-for-future-learning (PFL) lens that credits learners for being prepared to learn in a new setting.

Reviews and contests four situated-learning claims (including knowledge does not transfer between tasks), citing evidence that abstract training does transfer and that strong situativity claims are overstated.
Replies to Anderson et al. by arguing that what transfers is patterns of participation across situations, reframing transfer from a situative rather than purely cognitive standpoint.

Proposes a process model in which transfer is a cycle of constructing a context representation, generating a solution, and evaluating whether it makes sense, integrating cognitive and situative accounts.
Frames assessment as an evidentiary assessment triangle (cognition, observation, interpretation), arguing instruments should target models of how knowledge develops and can be applied.
Lays out evidence-centered design (ECD), making explicit the student, evidence, and task models that connect what we want to infer (e.g., transfer) to observable task performance.
Introduces the double-transfer assessment that embeds a learning resource into the transfer test, revealing PFL gains from invention activities that a standard sequestered transfer test misses.
Surveys dynamic-testing approaches that measure learning potential during guided instruction rather than static prior achievement, a near-relative of PFL transfer assessment.
Contrasts behaviorist/measurement assessment with a social-constructivist framework, arguing classroom assessment should be dynamic and embedded to support transferable understanding.
Argues for authentic performance assessment that requires students to apply knowledge to realistic, contextualized tasks rather than recognize answers, foregrounding transfer of competence.

Across five experiments using Duncker radiation problem, subjects who first read a structurally analogous military story rarely produced the convergence solution spontaneously, but did so far more often once given an explicit hint to use the story.

Adults who solve arithmetic problems fluently while grocery shopping or dieting fail equivalent school-format problems, showing that competence is bound to setting rather than transferring as decontextualized skill.

Meta-analysis of working-memory training studies found reliable near-transfer gains but no convincing evidence of far transfer to nonverbal ability, reading, or arithmetic when compared to treated controls.
A comprehensive meta-analysis found the far-transfer effect of video-game training on cognitive ability to be essentially null once methodological quality and active controls were accounted for.

Reviewing multiple domains (working memory, music, chess, exergames), the authors argue the overall far-transfer effect is null with little true between-domain variability, questioning whether the phenomenon exists at all.
Reviews why transfer appears so rare in the lab yet pervasive in everyday expertise, arguing that methodological framing and overly literal similarity criteria drive much of the documented pessimism.

Brief training in the law of large numbers increased both the frequency and quality of statistical reasoning on everyday problems in domains where the rule was never explicitly taught, showing domain-independent transfer of an abstract rule.

Expert programmers rely on reusable programming plans and rules of programming discourse; violating these conventions degraded expert comprehension toward novice levels, evidencing plan-based transferable knowledge.

A Transfer Tutor that explained R syntax and semantics in terms of programmers existing Python knowledge was used to study how prior-language knowledge scaffolds — and sometimes misleads — learning of a new language.

Analysis of Stack Overflow questions across 18 languages plus interviews found hundreds of cases of negative transfer, where faulty assumptions carried over from a known language interfered with learning a new one.
Maps cognitive-psychology theories of analogical transfer onto programming-language learning, proposing how comparison and alignment techniques could support teaching multiple languages.

Across 37 studies and 7,832 students the authors report a moderate overall transfer effect, with moderate effects for both near and far transfer of computational thinking, moderated by educational level and instructional factors.
Interleaving (shuffling) practice problems of different types rather than blocking them by topic markedly improved performance on a delayed test, despite feeling harder during practice.
Argues interleaving improves learning chiefly by requiring discrimination among similar concepts, building the category knowledge that supports later transfer to novel items.
Free-recall testing without feedback produced substantially better one-week retention than equivalent restudy, establishing the testing/retrieval-practice effect with prose materials.
Comparing two analogous cases (vs. studying them separately) helped novices abstract problem schemas and transfer negotiation strategies to a new face-to-face exercise.
Good learners generated many self-explanations while studying worked examples, refining the conditions for actions; poor learners did not, predicting later problem-solving success.
Gradually fading worked-out solution steps into problems-to-solve eases the example-to-problem transition and improves skill acquisition under a cognitive-load account.
Analyzing contrasting cases before instruction generated differentiated knowledge structures that prepared learners to understand a subsequent telling deeply, improving transfer.

Reviews desirable difficulties (spacing, interleaving, testing, varied practice) that slow apparent acquisition but enhance durable, transferable learning, and the metacognitive illusions that lead learners to avoid them.
Reconceptualizes validity as a unified construct-based judgment that must include the value implications of score meaning and the social consequences of score use (consequential validity).
An argument-based approach lays out the chain of inferences and assumptions from test responses to score interpretations and uses, then evaluates the plausibility of each link.
Generalizability-theory analysis shows large task-sampling variability in performance assessments, so many tasks are needed to generalize dependably from observed performance to the broader domain.
Defines systemic validity: a test is systemically valid if it induces instructional and learning-strategy changes that foster the very cognitive traits it purports to measure.
